{{Short description|Geometry problem}}
The '''distance''' (or '''perpendicular distance''') '''from a point to a line''' is the shortest [[Euclidean distance|distance]] from a fixed [[Point (geometry)|point]] to any point on a fixed infinite [[Line (mathematics)|line]] in [[Euclidean geometry]]. It is the length of the [[line segment]] that joins the point to the line and is [[perpendicular]] to the line. The formula for calculating it can be derived and expressed in several ways.

Knowing the shortest distance from a point to a line can be useful in various situations&mdash;for example, finding the shortest distance to reach a road, quantifying the scatter on a graph, etc. In [[Deming regression]], a type of linear [[curve fitting]], if the [[dependent and independent variables]] have equal variance, this results in [[orthogonal regression]] in which the degree of imperfection of the fit is measured for each data point as the perpendicular distance of the point from the regression line.

==Cartesian coordinates==
===Line defined by an equation===
In the case of a line in the plane given by the equation <math>ax + by + c = 0</math> where <math>a</math>, <math>b</math> and <math>c</math> are [[real number|real]] constants with <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> not both zero, the distance from the line to a point <math>(x_0,y_0)</math> is<ref>{{harvnb|Larson|Hostetler|2007|loc=p. 452}}</ref><ref>{{harvnb|Spain|2007}}</ref>{{rp|p.14}}

:<math>\operatorname{distance}(ax+by+c=0, (x_0, y_0)) = \frac{|ax_0+by_0+c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}. </math>

The point on this line that is closest to <math>(x_0,y_0)</math> has coordinates:<ref>{{harvnb|Larson|Hostetler|2007|loc=p. 522}}</ref>
:<math>x = \frac{b(bx_0 - ay_0)-ac}{a^2 + b^2} \text{ and } y = \frac{a(-bx_0 + ay_0) - bc}{a^2+b^2}</math>
or equivalently<blockquote><math>x = x_0 - a \frac{a x_0 + b y_0 + c}{a^2 + b^2}</math> and <math>y = y_0 - b \frac{a x_0 + b y_0 + c}{a^2 + b^2}</math></blockquote>'''Horizontal and vertical lines'''

In the general equation of a line, <math>ax + by + c = 0</math>, <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> cannot both be zero unless <math>c</math> is also zero; in that case, the equation does not define a line. If <math>a=0</math> and <math>b \neq 0</math>, the line is horizontal and has equation <math>y = -c/b</math>. The distance from <math>(x_0,y_0)</math> to this line is measured along a vertical line segment of length <math>|y_0 - (-c/b)| = |b y_0 + c| / |b|</math> in accordance with the formula. Similarly, for vertical lines <math>(b = 0)</math> the distance between the same point and the line is <math>|a x_0 + c| / |a|</math>, as measured along a horizontal line segment.

===Line defined by two points===
If the line passes through two points <math>P_1=(x_1,y_1)</math> and <math>P_2=(x_2,y_2)</math> then the distance of <math>(x_0,y_0)</math> from the line is:
:<math>\operatorname{distance}(P_1, P_2, (x_0, y_0)) = \frac{|(y_2-y_1)x_0-(x_2-x_1)y_0+x_2 y_1-y_2 x_1|}{\sqrt{(y_2-y_1)^2+(x_2-x_1)^2}}. </math>

The denominator of this expression is the distance between <math>P_1</math> and <math>P_2</math>. The numerator is twice the area of the triangle with its vertices at the three points, <math>(x_0,y_0)</math>, <math>P_1</math> and <math>P_2</math>. See: {{slink|Area of a triangle|Using coordinates}}. The expression is equivalent to <math display="inline">h=\frac{2A}{b}</math>, which can be obtained by rearranging the standard formula for the area of a triangle: <math display="inline">A=\frac{1}{2} bh</math>, where <math>b</math> is the length of a side, and <math>h</math> is the perpendicular height from the opposite vertex.

== Line defined by point and angle ==
If the line passes through the point <math>P = (P_x, P_y)</math> with angle <math>\theta</math>, then the distance of some point <math>(x_0,y_0)</math> to the line is
:<math>\operatorname{distance}(P, \theta, (x_0, y_0)) = |\cos(\theta)(P_y-y_0) -\sin(\theta)(P_x-x_0)| </math>

==Proofs==

===An algebraic proof===
This proof is valid only if the line is neither vertical nor horizontal, that is, we assume that neither <math>a</math> nor <math>b</math> in the equation of the line is zero.

The line with equation <math>ax + by + c = 0</math> has slope <math>-a/b</math>, so any line perpendicular to it will have slope <math>b/a</math> (the negative reciprocal). Let <math>(m, n)</math> be the point of intersection of the line <math>ax + by + c = 0</math> and the line perpendicular to it which passes through the point <math>(x_0, y_0)</math>. The line through these two points is perpendicular to the original line, so  
:<math>\frac{y_0 - n}{x_0 - m}=\frac{b}{a}.</math>
Thus,
<math>a(y_0 -n) - b(x_0 - m) = 0,</math>
and by squaring this equation we obtain:
:<math>a^2(y_0 - n)^2 + b^2(x_0 - m)^2 = 2ab(y_0 - n)(x_0 - m).</math>

Now consider,
:<math> (a(x_0 - m) + b(y_0 - n))^2 = a^2(x_0 - m)^2 + 2ab(y_0 -n)(x_0 - m) + b^2(y_0 - n)^2 = (a^2 + b^2)((x_0 - m)^2 + (y_0 - n)^2)</math>
using the above squared equation. But we also have,
:<math> (a(x_0 - m) + b(y_0 - n))^2 = (ax_0 + by_0 - am -bn )^2 = (ax_0 + by_0 + c)^2</math>
since (''m'', ''n'') is on ''ax'' + ''by'' + ''c'' = 0.
Thus,
:<math>(a^2 + b^2)((x_0 - m)^2 + (y_0 - n)^2) = (ax_0 + by_0 + c)^2 </math>
and we obtain the length of the line segment determined by these two points,
:<math>d=\sqrt{(x_0 - m)^2+(y_0 - n)^2}= \frac{|ax_0+ by_0 +c|}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}.</math><ref>Between Certainty and Uncertainty: Statistics and Probability in Five Units With Notes on Historical Origins and Illustrative Numerical Examples</ref>

===A geometric proof===
[[File:point-to-line2.svg|thumb|Diagram for geometric proof]]

This proof is valid only if the line is not horizontal or vertical.<ref>{{harvnb|Ballantine|Jerbert|1952}} do not mention this restriction in their article</ref>

Drop a perpendicular from the point <math>P</math> with coordinates <math>(x_0, y_0)</math> to the line with equation <math>Ax + By + C = 0</math>. Label the foot of the perpendicular <math>R</math>. Draw the vertical line through <math>P</math> and label its intersection with the given line <math>S</math>. At any point <math>T</math> on the line, draw a [[right triangle]] <math>TVU</math> whose sides are horizontal and vertical line segments with [[hypotenuse]] <math>TU</math> on the given line and horizontal side of length <math>|B|</math> (see diagram). The vertical side of <math>\triangle TVU</math> will have length <math>|A|</math> since the line has slope <math>-A/B</math>.

<math>\triangle PRS</math> and <math>\triangle TVU</math> are [[similar triangles]], since they are both right triangles and <math>\angle PSR \cong \angle TUV</math> since they are corresponding angles of a transversal to the parallel lines <math>PS</math> and <math>UV</math> (both are vertical lines).<ref>If the two triangles are on opposite sides of the line, these angles are congruent because they are alternate interior angles.</ref> Corresponding sides of these triangles are in the same ratio, so:
:<math>\frac{|\overline{PR}|}{|\overline{PS}|} = \frac{|\overline{TV}|}{|\overline{TU}|}.</math>
If point <math>S</math> has coordinates <math>(x_0,m)</math> then <math>|PS| = |y_0 - m|</math> and the distance from <math>P</math> to the line is:
:<math> |\overline{PR} | = \frac{|y_0 - m||B|}{\sqrt{A^2 + B^2}}.</math>
Since <math>S</math> is on the line, we can find the value of <math>m</math>,
:<math>m = \frac{-Ax_0 - C}{B},</math>
and finally obtain:<ref>{{harvnb|Ballantine|Jerbert|1952}}</ref>
:<math> |\overline{PR}| = \frac{|Ax_0 + By_0 + C|}{\sqrt{A^2 + B^2}}.</math>

A variation of this proof is to place <math>V</math> at <math>P</math> and compute the area of the triangle <math> \triangle UVT</math> two ways to obtain that <math>D|\overline{TU}| = |\overline{VU}||\overline{VT}|</math>
where <math>D</math> is the altitude of <math>\triangle UVT</math> drawn to the hypoteneuse of <math>\triangle UVT</math> from <math>P</math>.  The distance formula can then used to express <math>|\overline{TU}|</math>, <math>|\overline{VU}|</math>, and <math>|\overline{VT}|</math>in terms of the coordinates of <math>P</math> and the coefficients of the equation of the line to get the indicated formula.{{citation needed|date=April 2015}}

===A vector projection proof===
[[File:vectorpoint-to-line.svg|250px|left|Diagram for vector projection proof]]

Let <math>P</math> be the point with coordinates <math>(x_0, y_0)</math> and let the given line have equation <math>ax + by + c = 0</math>. Also, let <math>Q = (x_1, y_1)</math> be any point on this line and <math>n</math> the vector <math>(a, b)</math> starting at point <math>Q</math>. The vector '''n''' is perpendicular to the line, and the distance <math>d</math> from point <math>P</math> to the line is equal to the length of the orthogonal projection of <math>\overrightarrow{QP}</math> on '''n'''. The length of this projection is given by:
:<math>d = \frac{|\overrightarrow{QP} \cdot \mathbf{n}|}{\| \mathbf{n}\|}.</math>
Now,
:<math> \overrightarrow{QP} = (x_0 - x_1, y_0 - y_1),</math> so <math> \overrightarrow{QP} \cdot \mathbf{n} = a(x_0 - x_1) + b(y_0 - y_1)</math> and <math> \| \mathbf{n} \| = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2},</math>
thus
:<math> d = \frac{|a(x_0 - x_1) + b(y_0 - y_1)|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}.</math>
Since <math>Q</math> is a point on the line, <math>c = -ax_1 - by_1</math>, and so,<ref>{{harvnb|Anton|1994|loc=pp. 138-9}}</ref>
:<math> d = \frac{|ax_0 + by_0 + c|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2}}.</math>

== Another formula ==
It is possible to produce another expression to find the shortest distance of a point to a line. This derivation also requires that the line is not vertical or horizontal.

The point <math>P</math> is given with coordinates <math>(x_0, y_0)</math>.
The equation of a line is given by <math>y=mx+k</math>. The equation of the normal of that line which passes through the point <math>P</math> is given <math>y=\frac{x_0-x}{m}+y_0</math>.

The point at which these two lines intersect is the closest point on the original line to the point <math>P</math>. Hence:
:<math>mx+k=\frac{x_0-x}{m}+y_0.</math>
We can solve this equation for <math>x</math>,
:<math>x=\frac{x_0+my_0-mk}{m^2+1}.</math>
The <math>y</math> coordinate of the point of intersection can be found by substituting this value of <math>x</math> into the equation of the original line,
:<math>y=m\frac{(x_0+my_0-mk)}{m^2+1}+k.</math>

Using the equation for finding the distance between <math>2</math> points, <math>d=\sqrt{(X_2-X_1)^2+(Y_2-Y_1)^2}</math>, we can deduce that the formula to find the shortest distance between a line and a point is the following:

:<math>d=\sqrt{ \left( {\frac{x_0 + m y_0-mk}{m^2+1}-x_0 } \right) ^2 + \left( {m\frac{x_0+m y_0-mk}{m^2+1}+k-y_0 }\right) ^2 } = \frac{|k + m x_0 - y_0|}\sqrt{1 + m^2} .</math>

Recalling that <math>m = -a/b</math> and <math>k = -c/b </math> for the line with equation <math>ax + by + c = 0</math>, a little algebraic simplification reduces this to the standard expression.<ref>{{harvnb|Larson|Hostetler|2007|loc=p. 522}}</ref>

==Vector formulation==
[[File:Distance from a point to a line.svg|thumb|300px|Illustration of the vector formulation.]]

The equation of a line can be given in [[Euclidean vector|vector]] form:

: <math> \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{a} + t\mathbf{n}</math>

Here {{math|'''a'''}} is the position of a point on the line, and {{math|'''n'''}} is a  [[unit vector]] in the direction of the line. Then as scalar <math>t</math> varies, {{math|'''x'''}} gives the [[locus (mathematics)|locus]] of the line.

The distance of an arbitrary point {{math|'''p'''}} to this line is given by

: <math>\operatorname{distance}(\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{a} + t\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{p}) = \| (\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{p}) - ((\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{p}) \cdot  \mathbf{n})\mathbf{n} \|. </math>

This formula can be derived as follows: <math>\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{p}</math> is a vector from {{math|'''p'''}} to the point {{math|'''a'''}} on the line. Then <math>(\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{p}) \cdot  \mathbf{n}</math> is the projected length onto the line and so
:<math>((\mathbf{a} - \mathbf{p}) \cdot  \mathbf{n})\mathbf{n}</math>
is a vector that is the [[projection (linear algebra)|projection]] of <math>\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{p}</math> onto the line. Thus
:<math>(\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{p}) - ((\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{p}) \cdot  \mathbf{n})\mathbf{n}</math>
is the component of <math>\mathbf{a}-\mathbf{p}</math> perpendicular to the line. The distance from the point to the line is then just the [[norm (mathematics)|norm]] of that vector.<ref>{{cite web|last=Sunday|first=Dan|title=Lines and Distance of a Point to a Line|url=http://geomalgorithms.com/a02-_lines.html|archive-url=https://archive.today/20131206184414/http://geomalgorithms.com/a02-_lines.html|url-status=usurped|archive-date=December 6, 2013|publisher=softSurfer|accessdate=6 December 2013}}</ref> This more general formula is not restricted to two dimensions.

== Another vector formulation ==

If the line (<math>l</math>) goes through point <math>A</math> and has a [[Euclidean vector|direction vector]] <math>\vec u</math>, the distance between point <math>P</math> and line (<math>l</math>) is
: <math>d(\mathrm{P}, (l))= \frac{\left\|\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AP}} \times\vec u\right\|}{\|\vec u\|}</math>
where <math>\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AP}} \times\vec u</math> is the [[cross product]] of the vectors <math>\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AP}}</math> and <math>\vec u</math> and where <math>\|\vec u\|</math> is the vector norm of <math>\vec u</math>.

<math>\overrightarrow{\mathrm{AP}}=P-A</math>

Note that cross products only exist in dimensions <math>3</math> and <math>7</math> and trivially in dimensions <math>0</math> and <math>1</math> (where the cross product is constant <math>0</math>).
